s1: [calm, clear product narration] Every engineering team knows this ticket. It's assigned to you... it isn't yours... so you pass it on. In VS Code, one thousand six hundred and seventy-eight issues were handed on like that in four and a half months. Every handoff is knowledge: this kind of issue goes to that person. Nobody keeps it. Handoff Graph does.
s2a: [calm, clear product narration] Here's a real bug from VS Code. The triage bot would give it to one engineer. But the graph remembers that this engineer has passed issues like it to a colleague, and the issue text agrees. So it routes straight there... and shows the path. Five of the hundred and fifty-one issues the bot gave them went that way.
s2b: [calm, clear product narration] This one is too close to call. Memory points to more than one person, and the text doesn't settle it. So instead of guessing... it asks a human, and says why.
s2c: [calm, clear product narration] And here, memory says this engineer keeps issues like this one. Two hundred and thirty-eight of four hundred and five. So it leaves the bot's pick alone. Same agent. Three different decisions. Each one backed by a path in the graph.
s3: [calm, clear product narration] This is the memory, in FalkorDB. Every reassignment becomes a timestamped HANDED OFF edge between two people. Two agents share this graph. The learner is the only one that writes. The router only reads... and only what was true before the issue arrived. Every query filters on time, so a decision can never see the future. And the model never writes Cypher. It gets a small, fixed set of tools.
s4: [calm, clear product narration] We tested this on real VS Code triage, replayed in time order, on two periods the system never saw during development. Each one, run once. Same AI model. Same decision code. With and without graph memory. Without memory, it gives up and hands sixty-six percent of issues to a human. With memory... four percent. Right owner on the first try: eighteen percent without memory. Seventy-four percent with it. Microsoft's dedicated triage classifier, built for this one repo, gets seventy-seven. And the second period tells the same story.
s5: [calm, clear product narration] It doesn't beat that classifier on a first guess, and we checked why. Most handoffs depend on workload and absences that you can't see when an issue arrives. And memory about people goes stale fast. Thirty-eight percent in July... thirteen percent a month later. So the learner keeps learning from every new handoff.
s6: [calm, clear product narration] It's a live MCP server too, so Claude Code, or any MCP client, can route issues with it. The code, the data, and every number are open. Handoff Graph... built on FalkorDB.
